episode_title: Ebola in Leiden, a Box 3 Retreat, and the Bolle Jos Aid Freeze
description: An aid worker with Ebola is being treated in strict isolation in Leiden, and the finance minister backs down on taxing small savers. Brussels and The Hague give different reasons for freezing aid to Sierra Leone. Plus Katwijk's giant pill factory, a new test for freelancers, rivers too shallow to measure, and a replica VOC ship that's about to be driven over a dike.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: An aid worker with Ebola is being treated in strict isolation in Leiden. The finance minister backs down on taxing small savers. And Brussels stops paying Sierra Leone, but whose reason do you believe?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Plus a seventeenth-century ship that's about to be driven over a dike.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's Friday, the second of October. I'm Maya.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And I'm Sam. This is Dutch Daily Briefing.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: We start in Leiden, where a patient with Ebola is being treated in strict isolation.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Who is it?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: An aid worker for Médecins Sans Frontières, Doctors Without Borders, who was infected in the Democratic Republic of Congo. A French private plane flew them in. That's about nine and a half hours in the air. It landed at Schiphol around a quarter to eight last night, and the Koninklijke Marechaussee, the Royal Military Police, escorted the patient to the LUMC, Leiden University Medical Center.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Do we know anything else about them?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Their identity, sex, nationality and condition haven't been released. The hospital and MSF both say there's no risk to other patients, visitors or the public, and visiting hours are unchanged. Health Minister Sophie Hermans says the LUMC is ready for exactly this.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And it's worth knowing that Ebola doesn't spread through the air. It spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of someone who's sick. We've done this before, too. In 2014, a Nigerian UN peacekeeper from Liberia was treated at UMC Utrecht, and he was cured.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: How bad is it in Congo?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It's the largest Ebola outbreak ever recorded there. It was declared in May in Ituri province, which is still the worst hit, and it's spread to North Kivu and beyond. There are more than eight thousand confirmed cases and nearly four thousand deaths.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And MSF says the true toll is probably higher. It's a rare strain called Bundibugyo, and there's no approved vaccine or treatment for it.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Which tells you what aid workers there are up against. There's no word yet on how this patient is doing.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Now, the budget debate, and a climbdown on taxing your savings.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Yesterday we told you MPs from all sides, even in the coalition, were rejecting a plan to cut the tax-free return in box three. That's the tax on savings and investments.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Well, Finance Minister Eelco Heinen has blinked. He called the criticism a 'clear signal' and says he's prepared to set a different threshold to spare small savers and investors. He admitted he'd underestimated how many people would start paying. Estimates say around eight hundred and fifty thousand.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So what's the new threshold?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: He didn't say, and he didn't say how he'd pay for it either. Finding the money elsewhere is 'enormously complicated', he said, with 'not many dials to turn'. He'll also look again at next year's cut, which roughly halves the tax-free allowance, but he made no promise to drop it. He wants clarity by the Tax Plan debate in two weeks.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Why the quick retreat? It's a minority cabinet. It needs opposition votes to pass its budget, and that gives the opposition real leverage.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: There's also a fallback cut to education of up to one point two billion euros a year. Heinen says it's 'technically booked', but it won't happen if employers and unions reach a social accord, a classic polder deal.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And the cabinet still has about three billion euros in savings to find. So if you've got money in the bank, watch that Tax Plan debate.

segments.title: EU aid freeze and Bolle Jos

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Next, an EU aid freeze in West Africa, with a Dutch fugitive at the heart of it.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The European Commission has stopped budget support to Sierra Leone, with immediate effect. That's eighteen million euros this year for food programmes, education and infrastructure. And Justice Minister David van Weel says it's because Sierra Leone won't extradite Jos Leijdekkers, better known as Bolle Jos.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Remind us who he is.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: He's often called the most wanted criminal in the Low Countries. He was sentenced in absentia to twenty-four years here for cocaine trafficking and an attempted murder, and to more than a hundred years in Belgium. He's reported to have a child with the Sierra Leonean president's daughter.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Van Weel says Sierra Leone 'can solve this within twenty-four hours' by arresting and extraditing him. The Netherlands also wants next year's payment of twenty-two and a half million stopped.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: But Brussels tells it differently.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It does. NOS reports that Van Weel's comments irritated the Commission. Officially, it's a technical matter of 'administrative errors', which the Commission hasn't spelled out. Commissioner Magnus Brunner would only add: 'We need Sierra Leone's cooperation. That is what this is about.'

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And there's a legal reason for that caution. Budget support deals are binding contracts, and extradition isn't one of the conditions. So suspending payments over it wouldn't be allowed.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: What does Sierra Leone say?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Information Minister Chernor Bah says it's procedural, about an amended financing agreement, and the payments are now proposed for 2027 and 2028. The government calls public pressure and media campaigns 'not conducive' to judicial cooperation. There's no extradition treaty, but both countries have signed a UN convention against organised crime that covers extradition.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Pressure here has grown since last month's deadly attack on a farm in Overasselt, which is believed to be linked to the drug trade. And EU justice ministers are now discussing entry bans and asset freezes for criminals hiding outside Europe.

segments.title: Katwijk says yes to Eli Lilly

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Back near Leiden now, where Katwijk has said yes to a giant American pill factory.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Katwijk's council voted twenty-eight to four last night to give Eli Lilly a building permit. It's a three-billion-dollar plant by a lake called the Valkenburgse Meer.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Lilly makes some of the world's best-selling diabetes and obesity drugs. This plant will make pills, including its GLP-1 pill orforglipron, and it should bring about five hundred jobs. CEO David Ricks says he picked Katwijk for the nearby airports and the Leiden Bio Science Park.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Not everyone's thrilled, though.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: No. Hundreds of residents asked for an advisory referendum. The council turned that down the same evening, partly because it had to decide on the permit this week. People worry about safety and about the views and recreation at the lake, but above all about water. The plant should use about eight hundred thousand litres of drinking water a day. That's roughly what every household in neighbouring Valkenburg uses.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And energy?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: The grid's full. Netcongestie, or grid congestion, means new businesses in much of the country wait years for a connection. So at first Lilly will make its own electricity with gas turbines.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: KiesKatwijk and GemeenteBelangen were among the no votes, but most of the council judged that the economic benefits outweigh the concerns.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And it's not done yet. Lilly still needs permits to start production and to discharge wastewater. It's been aiming to start production in 2030.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Now, if you freelance here, listen up: there's a draft law on who counts as self-employed.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Ah, the zzp'er question. That stands for zelfstandige zonder personeel, self-employed without staff, and there are more than a million of them. The worry is schijnzelfstandigheid, false self-employment. That's when someone works like an employee but is hired as a freelancer to avoid payroll taxes. The tax authority cracked down, and many clients stopped hiring freelancers at all.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Like California's AB5 fight. So Minister Thierry Aartsen has published the Zelfstandigenwet, the Self-Employed Persons Act. It has two tests: are you genuinely self-employed, and what's the working relationship like?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: In plain terms?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: You're registered with the KvK, the Chamber of Commerce, and you have a VAT number and a business bank account. You send invoices. You've had at least three different clients over two years, and you're looking for more. And you decide where, when and how you work, unless the job's tied to a place, like a building site.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And there's a minimum spend on things employees don't need, like disability insurance, a pension or liability cover. The amount's still to be agreed. Aartsen says it mustn't be too high, but it mustn't be a 'wassen neus', an empty gesture, either.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: How many will pass?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Aartsen reckons two-thirds to three-quarters already do, or could fairly easily. So a quarter to a third don't, yet. If you pass, you won't have to fear back-tax claims.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Most freelancer groups welcome it in principle. ZZP Nederland wants workable criteria, and it warns that clients mustn't shut freelancers out just to be safe. Earlier this year, the union FNV Zelfstandigen said it saw 'no added value' in the law.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: There's no transition period. But you can comment on the draft until the twenty-ninth of October, and it won't take effect before 2028.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Next, the rivers in the east of the country, which are now too shallow to measure.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Too shallow to measure? How?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Rijkswaterstaat, the national waterways agency, measures the river with survey boats. But in parts of the IJssel, the Nederrijn, the Pannerdensch Kanaal and the Waal, the water's now less than a hundred and twenty-five centimetres deep. Most survey boats sit deeper than that.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So the boats that measure the river can't get onto the river.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Pretty much. Only three shallower boats are left, and they're needed elsewhere too. So skippers don't get the shallowest point in the channel, which tells them how much cargo they can carry without running aground. Now they have to judge for themselves or pay for commercial data.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And these rivers are the freight route from Rotterdam into Germany. Some ships are taking detours of up to three hundred kilometres, and Rotterdam says cargo to the Rhine has halved compared with a year ago. Shipping a tonne to Cologne went from about seventeen euros in June to eighty in August.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Rijkswaterstaat says things won't get much better or much worse until it rains upstream, mostly outside the country. And it warns that an unusually warm sea could bring a very wet autumn, and then high water.

segments.title: Young Amsterdammers: less drink, more ketamine

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Here in Amsterdam, there's a new report on what young people are drinking, and what they're taking.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: It's the yearly Antenne Amsterdam monitor, done for Jellinek, the city's best-known addiction care organisation. Young people are drinking less, but ketamine use in nightlife has risen sharply since 2024.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It's based on a survey of nearly twelve hundred vocational students, interviews with nightlife insiders, and almost five thousand drug samples. Here you can hand drugs in anonymously to have them tested.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Ketamine, MDMA and other powders go for about twenty-five to thirty euros a gram, delivered to your door. Demand for 3-MMC, a synthetic stimulant, has barely dipped despite last year's ban, and pills sold as 3-MMC often contain something else.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: But laughing gas has almost vanished since it was banned in 2023.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Among the students, about half have vaped, and online gambling is becoming normal. Eighteen percent gambled online in the past year, up from six percent in 2021. The question was worded differently this time, though, so it's a rough comparison.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: So are they swapping beer for cheaper drugs?

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Jellinek's Jacqueline Krouwel says no, Gen Z is just drinking less. If you're worried about yourself or someone else, Jellinek's helpline takes calls in English on weekday afternoons.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Maya, there's a medical first from Nijmegen that's been a long time coming.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Tell me.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Surgeons at Radboudumc, the university hospital there, can now rebuild the clitoris when part of it has to be removed because of vulvar cancer. Until now, the wound was simply closed and the clitoris disappeared under the skin.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: How does it work?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: While removing the tumour, they free the nerve bundles and move them to form a new tip, covered with tissue from inside the cheek. It adds about fifteen minutes to the operation. In a first study of twenty-three women, ninety percent could have a clitoral orgasm again three to six months after surgery.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And it all started because a patient asked if it was possible. So why 'a long time coming'?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Men with penile cancer have had a comparable reconstruction for almost forty years.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Wow. Well, now all nine Dutch hospitals that treat vulvar cancer will learn the technique.

segments.title: The Batavia heads for dry land

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: In Lelystad today, a ship's going to be driven over a dike. Yes, driven.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The Batavia! It's a full-size replica of a seventeenth-century ship from the VOC, the Dutch East India Company. Yesterday tugboats towed it across the IJ from the NDSM wharf in Amsterdam-Noord, sitting in a steel frame on a pontoon, while crowds watched.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Then it crossed the Markermeer to Museum Batavialand. Today it rolls off the pontoon and over the dike, and it'll sit next to the museum for good. After about thirty years afloat, the hull has wood rot.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Can you still go aboard?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Not yet. It'll be restored in stages, and the museum plans to let visitors back on when it reopens in 2028.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: The original had a grim story, didn't it?

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: It was wrecked off Australia on its maiden voyage in 1628. Among the survivors there was a mutiny, and then a massacre.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: This one fared better. Queen Beatrix christened it in 1995, and now it gets a well-earned retirement on dry land.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: And if you're staying in Amsterdam tonight, I've got three ideas.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: Go on.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Camera Japan, the biggest Japanese film festival in the Benelux, is at LAB111 in Oud-West. There are nineteen films, from anime and arthouse to classics, plus food, music and dance. Drop in any time between half past twelve and ten tonight. It runs until Sunday, but times could still change, so check their website.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: I'm tempted by jazz. Saxophonist Benjamin Herman's European Alto Festival is at the Bimhuis in Oost at half past eight. It's a tribute to Piet Noordijk, with Spain's Irene Reig and Scotland's Rachael Cohen. One night only.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: Or there's Afrovibes, now in its twenty-third year, at De Brakke Grond in the centre from half past seven. It's dance, theatre, music and spoken word by artists from Africa and the diaspora.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And if you miss it tonight, it moves to the Bijlmer Parktheater and Framer Framed over the weekend.

lines.speaker: Sam
lines.text: That's it for today. I'm Sam.

lines.speaker: Maya
lines.text: And I'm Maya. This has been Dutch Daily Briefing. Have a lovely weekend.
